text.p: A groundswell of optimism that a deal on the key EU budget stability pact was in sight robbed the mark of the gains it had made since France cast doubt over the whole EMU project early this week. Satellite currencies sank against the mark after France said on Monday that it needed more time to study the pact, which is due to be ratified at next week's EU summit in Amsterdam.

But after talks with French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and President Jacques Chirac on Thursday, European Commission President Jacques Santer said "all elements are on the table" to enable French ratification of the pact.
Jospin said his new Socialist government's concerns on Europe had been understood and progress was being made.

EU Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said he believed Europe would be able to reach a deal in Amsterdam, by making more explicit reference to the need to coordinate economic policies across Europe and fight to reduce unemployment.

The mark was trading at 982.70/10 Italian lire and 3.3761/66 French francs at 1431 GMT. That was well below Wednesday's European closes of 986.05/55 and 3.3822/27 and compared with levels of 986.00/30 and 3.3763/66 last Friday -- before France's bombshell triggered a flight into marks.

Analysts said the apparent move towards agreement on the stability pact -- aimed at enforcing budgetary discipline after EMU begins -- had persuaded the market that the political will to launch the euro on time was undimmed.

"This is what's encouraging people to take a much more sanguine view on the mark crosses and to go back to the old convergence trend, particularly for the likes of Italy and Spain," said Stephen Hannah, director of research at IBJ.
The Spanish peseta firmed to 84.53/55 per mark from late Wednesday's 84.58/60, above last Friday's 84.57/59 close.
Concern that EMU could be delayed tends to buoy the mark as players see the risk recede that it will be subsumed into a weaker single currency.

On the other hand, talk of a broad-based first wave of EMU, encompassing countries such as Italy and Spain, usually has the opposite effect as the market weighs up the prospect that the German unit will give way to a softer euro.

This month's election victory for the French left wing -- which wants to see a broad start to EMU -- has stoked fears of a weak euro, as have Germany's difficulties in plugging its budget holes to qualify for monetary union.

Bonn's controversial proposal to revalue gold and currency assets fuelled those concerns as the market fretted that Germany was looking to fudge the EMU entry criteria, opening the way for "creative accounting" by other aspiring participants.
The Bundesbank, which has sharply attacked the government's revaluation plans, today welcomed efforts to resolve its row with Bonn and said it hoped for a compromise soon.

The market's conviction that political will would override economic realities was reflected in its impassive reaction to a report from the OECD, which predicted that Germany, France and Italy would all miss the EMU deficit target this year.
In its economic outlook, the OECD forecast 1997 deficit/GDP ratios of 3.2 percent for those countries, above the 3.0 percent limit laid down in the Maastricht Treaty on monetary union.
The report predicted Germany and France would see their deficits fall to 2.7 and 3.0 percent respectively in 1998, but Italy's budget gap was forecast to widen to 3.8.
The market will be keeping a close eye on the Franco-German summit in the western French city of Poitiers on Friday, ahead of the Amsterdam summit on June 16-17.
